newsitem.title: USA: Clinton strongly refuses to stop raising money.
newsitem.headline: Clinton strongly refuses to stop raising money.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday passionately refused to cut back on raising money for Democrats in the face of investigations into last year's campaign financing.

At a news conference, Clinton interrupted a reporter in the middle of a question about campaign financing to give a lecture on why he continues to solicit the kind of large, unregulated "soft money" contributions that he himself has proposed banning.
"I certainly do, and I'm proud of it," he said. "I plead guilty to that. I don't believe in unilateral disarmament."
Clinton has travelled far and wide in recent months to help the debt-ridden Democratic Party reload for 1998 midterm congressional races.
On Thursday, Clinton is to attend a fund-raising event in Washington for the Democratic National Committee. There is another one next week in St. Louis.
The reason he said he could not stop raising money was because the Republicans will not either.
"We live in a competitive world," he said.
He complained that opposition Republicans will still raise and spend twice as much money as Democrats. He charged they "raise more money from non-citizens."

That was a slap at hearings in the Republican-controlled Senate Governmental Affairs Committee that have focused mostly on Democratic financing abuses, including illegal contributions from foreign sources.
It was revealed during the hearings last month that Republicans received some support from questionable foreign sources as well.
The hearings are to resume in the fall after an August recess. Meantime, the Justice Department is conducting its own investigation into last year's efforts.

The chairman of the Senate committee, Tennessee Republican Fred Thompson, has complained he cannot get to the bottom of the fund-raising controversy because many important witnesses were overseas or were refusing to testify.

Two of those are former Little Rock, Ark., restaurant owner Yah Lin "Charlie" Trie, who is now in China, and former Democratic fund-raiser John Huang, who has said he will not testify without immunity from prosecution.
Asked if he would appeal for them to come tell their story, Clinton was less than enthusiastic.
He repeated his appeal for everyone to cooperate and said the State Department has tried to work with the committee on persuading Trie to come back.
"So I don't know what else we can do on that," he said.
A spokesman for the Republican majority on the Senate committee, Paul Clark, said Clinton has not been as cooperative as he says.
"The White House has not been enormously cooperative in response to our inquiries," he said. "Just last week we had to subpoena the White House just to get documents sent to us in a timely fashion.

"It seems to be a practice on the part of the White House and the DNC to largely stonewall the investigation here in the Senate and that's something the president didn't address in his remarks," Clark said.
The president repeated his desire to see Congress approve campaign finance reform legislation this year.
"We'd be better off if we had ceilings on contributions to the political parties," he said. "We'd be better off if somebody couldn't give a million dollars to a political party at one pop."
